viva.question: How do you manage unstable tachyarrhythmia?
viva.bridge: A synchronised shock lands on the R wave so it cannot fall on the T wave and cause VF. Next: how many joules for each rhythm →
viva.lesson:
Go back to the two shocks from the beginning.

Think about what the ventricle is doing across one heartbeat. At the R wave, the whole ventricle is depolarising together. Every cell has just fired, and every cell is refractory. A shock that lands here can't start anything new. It simply resets the lot.

Now move along to the T wave. The ventricle is repolarising, and it doesn't do that evenly. Some regions have already recovered and can fire again. Their neighbours are still refractory. For a brief moment the muscle is a patchwork. A shock landing on that patchwork excites the recovered regions, the wavefront meets refractory tissue, bends around it, and comes back on itself. That's re-entry, and in a ventricle it becomes fibrillation. This is the R on T phenomenon, and that stretch of the T wave is called the vulnerable period.

{{pic}}

So the machine does something simple. In sync mode it watches the ECG, finds each R wave, and puts a marker on it. You can see those markers in the picture, and on the real screen. When you press the button, it doesn't fire at once. It waits for the next R wave and fires on its peak.

[[A synchronised shock is delivered on the peak of the R wave, so it cannot fall on the T wave and start ventricular fibrillation.]]

That's cardioversion. It's used for rhythms that have an organised QRS and a pulse: ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter.

Defibrillation is the same shock with no timing at all. It's used for ventricular fibrillation and for polymorphic VT. And the logic is worth more than the list. In VF there is no R wave. There's nothing to synchronise to, and nothing left to protect, because the worst has already happened. [[Synchronisation is needed only when there is an organised R wave to find and a perfusing rhythm to lose.]]

One practical consequence. Because the machine waits for an R wave, there's a short delay after you press. Keep the button held until it fires. Residents let go early, nothing happens, and they think the machine has failed.

So now we know when the shock lands. How big should it be?

p12.question: Unstable or stable: the tachycardia algorithm and the shock
p12.bridge: Timing and energy are set. Now the bedside: who is shocked at once, and what must be ready.
p12.lesson:
The timing is fixed. Now the size of the shock, and here the twenty twenty-five guideline changed the numbers. That matters, because two bank keys still carry the old ones.

Start with why different rhythms need different energies. A shock ends an arrhythmia by depolarising enough muscle at once that the circuit has nowhere left to go. How much current that takes depends on how much tissue is involved. AF is many small wavelets wandering across both atria, so you have to capture a large mass of atrium in one go. Flutter is one large circuit in the atrium. A regular SVT is a small circuit through the node. Monomorphic VT is one organised ventricular circuit with a clean R wave.

The old teaching was to start low and climb. What changed is the evidence on starting low. Low-energy shocks failed more often, and worse, they sometimes provoked the next arrhythmia: VF when cardioverting AF, and AF when cardioverting flutter. A failed shock isn't free. It means another shock under sedation, more delay, and another chance of harm. Pooled biphasic trials found that two hundred joules gave over ninety per cent cumulative success, with no extra myocardial injury.

{{**AHA 2025, synchronised, biphasic**
AF | at least 200 J (class 2a)
Flutter | 200 J (class 2b)
Narrow regular SVT | 100 J
Monomorphic VT with a pulse | 100 J
Polymorphic VT | unsynchronised, defibrillation dose (class 1)}}

[[From twenty twenty-five, AF starts at two hundred joules or more and flutter at two hundred. Narrow regular SVT and monomorphic VT with a pulse start at one hundred. Sustained polymorphic VT is defibrillated, unsynchronised.]]

One point of honesty about the hundred. The guideline text gives a figure only for AF and flutter. The hundred joules for SVT and monomorphic VT comes from the algorithm chart, and it's what the keys use.

Now the traps. First, the old AF range. One grand test keys one hundred and twenty to two hundred joules for unstable AF, and a question bank item keys one hundred. In both, what's being tested is cardioversion over a drug, and that part is right. So pick cardioversion, and if two hundred or more is on the list, that's the current answer.

Second, polymorphic VT with a pulse. NEET's favourite wrong options are synchronised cardioversion at one hundred joules, and magnesium. The guideline treats every sustained polymorphic VT as unstable, whatever the QT, and gives an immediate unsynchronised shock. Magnesium belongs to one situation: torsades on a long QT that comes in runs and stops by itself. You'll meet it properly in the wide section.

You may see European numbers in a stem: maximum output for AF, seventy to one hundred and twenty joules for flutter and SVT, one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty for VT with a pulse. The bank keys follow the American numbers, so learn the box.

You've got the timing and the dose. What's left is the bedside: who gets shocked at once, and what you need around you.

viva.lesson:
This is a table card, and the table changed in twenty twenty-five.

Atrial fibrillation, two hundred joules. Atrial flutter, two hundred joules. Narrow-complex tachycardia, one hundred. Monomorphic VT with a pulse, one hundred. And polymorphic VT isn't cardioverted at all. It gets an unsynchronised, high-energy shock.

{{**Synchronised cardioversion, AHA 2025 (biphasic)**
AF | at least 200 J
Atrial flutter | 200 J
Narrow regular (SVT) | 100 J
Monomorphic VT with pulse | 100 J
Polymorphic VT | unsynchronised, high energy}}

The older teaching was one hundred and twenty to two hundred for AF, and fifty to one hundred for flutter. Both are now two hundred. Why go up? Because low-energy shocks turned out to be the risky ones. When AF was cardioverted at low energy, the shock was significantly more likely to provoke VF. And low-energy shocks for flutter were more likely to provoke AF. A shock too small to reset the whole heart can disorganise it instead.

[[AF and flutter, two hundred joules. Narrow regular tachycardia and monomorphic VT, one hundred. Polymorphic VT is defibrillated.]]

One honest detail, in case the panel pushes. In the guideline text itself, AHA gives joules only for AF, at least two hundred as a class two A recommendation, and for flutter, two hundred as class two B. The one hundred for the other two rhythms comes from AHA's electrical cardioversion algorithm. And the main tachycardia algorithm says to use your device's recommended energy, and if you don't know it, the maximum setting. If the first shock fails, you go up.

So we have the timing and the dose. What must be at the bedside before you press?

p12.question: Unstable or stable: the tachycardia algorithm and the shock
p12.bridge: Now the whole section in one patient: fast AF, low pressure, wet lungs, duration unknown.
p12.lesson:
Timing, energy, and now the doing of it. Four things on this card, and the questions come from three of them.

First, when to prepare to shock at once. The algorithm's number is a ventricular rate above one hundred and fifty. Why a rate? Because a reasonably healthy heart tolerates anything slower. If a patient is hypotensive at a rate of one hundred and twenty, the rhythm is very unlikely to be the cause. Something else is, sepsis or bleeding or hypoxia, and the heart is racing to compensate. Shocking a compensatory sinus tachycardia does nothing at all. So below about one hundred and fifty, look for the cause and treat that.

Second, what's at the bedside: a saturation monitor, suction, an IV line and intubation equipment. Each one answers a specific risk. Sedation can stop breathing or cause aspiration, and the shock itself can leave a bradycardia or VF.

Third, the prerequisites: consent, sedation and analgesia, and ruling out a left atrial clot. Take sedation first, because it was asked. The current guidance is that sedation is advisable in the awake patient, judged against how stable he is, and it must never dangerously delay the shock. The trap options are mandatory intubation, or an arterial line, before cardioversion. Neither is required, and both delay it.

Now the clot, which is the part asked most. In AF the atria don't contract, blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage, and after about forty-eight hours you must assume a clot has formed. Restore sinus rhythm and the atrium may throw it into the brain. So for AF of more than forty-eight hours, or of unknown duration, in a stable patient, you anticoagulate for three weeks first, or you look with a transoesophageal echo and cardiovert if the appendage is clear. Then comes the half people forget. After sinus rhythm returns on the ECG, the atrium is stunned and contracts poorly for weeks. New clot can still form.

[[Before elective cardioversion of AF beyond forty-eight hours: three weeks of anticoagulation, or a transoesophageal echo. After it: at least four weeks, whatever the stroke score, because the atrium stays stunned.]]

NEET's favourite wrong option is two or three weeks after. Three is the number before. Four is the number after, and seventy-eight per cent got it. Only then does the stroke score decide the long term.

And none of that applies to the unstable patient. Shock first, heparin alongside. The next card is exactly that patient.

Fourth, two procedural notes. Resynchronise after each shock, because many machines drop back to unsynchronised mode once they've fired. And if the machine can't find an R wave and the patient is crashing, don't wait: give an unsynchronised shock.

Now put the whole section into one patient.

viva.question: How do you manage unstable tachyarrhythmia?
viva.bridge: Sedate if you can, re-sync after every shock, and go unsynchronised if sync delays a dying patient. Next: the one rhythm never synchronised →
viva.lesson:
You're an anaesthetist, so read this card as a short anaesthetic in a shocked patient. Because that's what it is.

First, when. A ventricular rate of about one hundred and fifty or more, with instability, means prepare for immediate cardioversion. The cardioversion algorithm prints above one hundred and fifty, and the main tachycardia algorithm prints typically one hundred and fifty or more, so don't split that hair. Below that, it's generally not needed, for the reason you already know. The rate is probably the response, not the cause.

Second, what's at the bedside. Four things. A saturation monitor. Suction. A working IV line. And intubation equipment. You're about to sedate someone with a pressure of eighty and wet lungs, so you prepare for the airway you hope not to need.

Third, the prerequisites. Consent, where it can be had. Sedation and analgesia, because a shock in an awake patient is painful and remembered. In an unstable patient that means a small, titrated dose, and the algorithm's own wording is sedate whenever feasible. If he's barely conscious, you don't delay the shock for a syringe.

The card also lists ruling out a left atrial clot. Be careful here, because the source had it backwards. The clot risk belongs to AF or flutter that has lasted more than forty-eight hours, or whose duration is unknown. And the rule itself belongs to the stable patient. [[In an unstable patient, clot rules do not delay the shock. They are for stable, elective cardioversion.]]

Fourth, two procedural notes, and both are favourite viva points. Resynchronise after each cardioversion. Many machines drop back to defibrillation mode once they've fired. So if the first shock fails and you simply press again, your second shock may be unsynchronised, and it may land on a T wave.

And the opposite problem. Sometimes the machine can't find the R wave. The complexes are small, or wide, or so fast that it can't tell R from T. It sits there, charged, waiting. [[If synchronisation is delayed and the patient is critical, go immediately to unsynchronised shocks.]] A dying patient isn't made to wait for a marker.

And that brings us to the one rhythm where the machine can never find its R wave.
